title: Recruitment as a political problem
paragraphs: A monarchy must decide how people enter service. Offices cannot be filled by abstract rules alone; rulers rely on households, teachers, patrons, and institutions capable of identifying candidates. Early Goryeo inherited regional power networks from the preceding era, and those networks remained important as kings sought to strengthen the center. The introduction of civil service examinations in the tenth century belonged to that wider political problem.

Examinations offered a formal way to associate official service with learning and performance. They did not instantly create equal opportunity for the entire population. Access to education, elite connections, family standing, and resources continued to shape who could prepare for an examination and pursue a career.
